question_text: Find the order of the differential equation of the family of all circles with their centres at the origin.

insider_note: The family has exactly ONE arbitrary constant, the radius r, so exactly one differentiation is enough to eliminate it — that single differentiation is what fixes the order at 1.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write the family and differentiate
steps.margin_note: One mark. The family of circles centred at the origin is x² + y² = r², with r the one parameter.
steps.memory_tip: Centre at the origin means the equation has no x or y term of its own — only x², y² and the single constant r².
lines: The equation of the family of circles
with centre at the origin is x² + y²
steps.why: The family of all circles centred at the origin has exactly one arbitrary constant, the radius r, so a single differentiation is what will be needed to eliminate it from the equation.
common_mistakes: Writing the general circle equation x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 instead of the centre-at-origin family x² + y² = r².
Forgetting the chain rule on y², differentiating it as 2y instead of 2y·dy/dx.

steps.label: Simplify and state the order
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Dividing by 2 removes r entirely, so the order is fixed by how many derivatives were needed to do that — just one.
steps.memory_tip: Order counts differentiations needed to eliminate every arbitrary constant, not the highest power appearing — here one differentiation already did the job.
steps.why: Dividing the differentiated equation by 2 eliminates r completely (it was never explicitly present after differentiating), leaving an equation with only x, y and the first derivative — so the order is 1.
common_mistakes: Assuming a circle's D.E. must have order 2, by confusing this family (one constant) with the general 3-constant circle family.
Leaving the equation as 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0 and not simplifying, though the order would still read as 1 either way.
